subject: HEMA
stem: Which coagulation factor is known as the stable factor?
explanation: Factor VII is also known as proconvertin or the stable factor. It is a vitamin K-dependent factor of the extrinsic pathway. Reference: PubMed 40727517 (Factor VII, also known as stable factor or proconvertin).

subject: HEMA
stem: Hemophilia A is caused by a deficiency of which coagulation factor?
explanation: Hemophilia A is an X-linked deficiency of Factor VIII. Hemophilia B (Christmas disease) is a Factor IX deficiency. Reference: StatPearls, Bleeding Disorders (ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK541050) and Hemophilia B (ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK560792).

subject: HEMA
stem: Which formula is used to compute the mean corpuscular volume (MCV) in fL?
explanation: MCV = (Hct ÷ RBC count in millions/µL) × 10. Hgb ÷ RBC × 10 is MCH, and Hgb ÷ Hct × 100 is MCHC. Reference: StatPearls, Mean Corpuscular Volume (ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK545275).

subject: HEMA
stem: Howell-Jolly bodies are red cell inclusions composed of:
explanation: Howell-Jolly bodies are DNA remnants, often seen after splenectomy. Denatured Hgb = Heinz bodies; RNA = basophilic stippling; iron = Pappenheimer bodies. Reference: StatPearls, Erythrocyte Inclusions (ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK594259).

subject: HEMA
stem: Auer rods in blast cells are most characteristic of:
explanation: Auer rods are fused primary (azurophilic) granules found in myeloid blasts, so they point to AML rather than lymphoid leukemias. Reference: StatPearls, Laboratory Evaluation of Acute Leukemia (ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK611988).

subject: HEMA
stem: Which iron profile is typical of iron deficiency anemia?
choices: Low serum iron, high TIBC, low ferritin
Normal serum iron, TIBC, and ferritin
Low serum iron, low TIBC, high ferritin
explanation: Iron deficiency gives low serum iron, high TIBC, and low ferritin, with microcytic, hypochromic cells. Anemia of chronic disease has a high ferritin, and thalassemia has normal iron studies. Ferritin is an acute-phase reactant, so inflammation can hide a low value. Reference: StatPearls, Chronic Anemia (ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK568790) and Iron Deficiency and Microcytic Hypochromic Anemia (ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK560876).

subject: HEMA
stem: Anemia with macrocytosis and hypersegmented neutrophils on the smear suggests:
choices: Megaloblastic anemia from vitamin B12 or folate deficiency
explanation: Anemia with macrocytosis and hypersegmented neutrophils is megaloblastic anemia, mainly caused by vitamin B12 or folate deficiency. Reference: StatPearls, Macrocytic Anemia (ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK459295).

subject: HEMA
stem: The anticoagulant of choice for a CBC and peripheral blood smear is:
explanation: EDTA (lavender top) prevents clotting by binding calcium and preserves cell morphology, so it is used for the CBC and smear. Reference: StatPearls, Laboratory Tube Collection (ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK555991).

subject: HEMA
stem: For PT and aPTT, blood is drawn into a 3.2% sodium citrate (light blue) tube at a blood-to-citrate ratio of:
explanation: Citrate binds calcium to keep the sample from clotting. The tube must be filled to at least 90% so the 9:1 blood-to-citrate ratio is kept; underfilling falsely prolongs results, especially the aPTT. Reference: StatPearls, Prothrombin Time (ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK544269).

subject: HEMA
stem: Erythropoietin is produced mainly by the:
choices: Peritubular interstitial cells of the kidney
explanation: Most erythropoietin comes from peritubular interstitial fibroblasts in the kidney, released mainly in response to hypoxia. That is why chronic kidney disease causes anemia. Reference: StatPearls, Anemia (ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK499994).

subject: HEMA
stem: In a healthy adult, red blood cells are produced in the:
explanation: Hematopoiesis starts in the yolk sac, shifts to the fetal liver (and spleen), and the bone marrow takes over near the end of gestation. In adults it normally occurs only in the bone marrow. Reference: StatPearls, Embryology, Hematopoiesis (ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK544245).

subject: HEMA
stem: The first site of blood cell formation in the embryo is the:
explanation: Blood formation starts in the extraembryonic yolk sac; stem cells then seed the fetal liver (and spleen) before the bone marrow takes over. Reference: Lawrence et al., The Ontogeny of a Neutrophil: Mechanisms of Granulopoiesis and Homeostasis (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5813886).

subject: HEMA
stem: The last granulocyte stage that can still divide is the:
explanation: Young myelocytes keep the ability to proliferate; after this stage cell division stops and the cells only mature. Reference: Lawrence et al., The Ontogeny of a Neutrophil: Mechanisms of Granulopoiesis and Homeostasis (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5813886).

subject: HEMA
stem: The last NUCLEATED stage in red cell maturation is the:
explanation: Orthochromatic erythroblasts (normoblasts) expel their nuclei to become reticulocytes, which have no nucleus. Reference: Erythroid Enucleation: A gateway into a "bloody" world (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8147720).

subject: HEMA
stem: During terminal erythropoiesis, about how many mitoses does a proerythroblast undergo?
explanation: The proerythroblast undergoes 3 to 4 mitoses to form basophilic, polychromatic and orthochromatic erythroblasts, which gain hemoglobin as they mature. Reference: Erythroid Enucleation: A gateway into a "bloody" world (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8147720).

subject: HEMA
stem: Megakaryocytes become large and polyploid through:
explanation: In endomitosis the DNA is copied but the cell does not divide, giving one large polyploid nucleus. Cyclins and CDK inhibitors regulate this process. Reference: A modern overview of the process of platelet formation (thrombocytopoiesis) (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11493462).

subject: HEMA
stem: In granulocyte maturation, specific (secondary) granules first appear at the:
explanation: Azurophilic (primary) granules form in myeloblasts and promyelocytes; specific (secondary) granules form in myelocytes and metamyelocytes. Reference: Lawrence et al., The Ontogeny of a Neutrophil: Mechanisms of Granulopoiesis and Homeostasis (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5813886).

subject: HEMA
stem: The average life span of a red blood cell in circulation is about:
explanation: In humans, red cells have a life span of about 120 days. Reference: Erythroid Enucleation: A gateway into a "bloody" world (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8147720).

subject: HEMA
stem: Which CD marker identifies hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells?
explanation: CD34 is a widely used surface marker of human hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells. CD3 = T cells, CD19 = B cells, CD41 = megakaryocytes/platelets. Reference: Extramedullary Hematopoiesis of the Liver and Spleen (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8707658).

subject: HEMA
stem: Besides hereditary spherocytosis, spherocytes on a smear are also common in:
explanation: Spherocytes alone do not prove hereditary spherocytosis, because immune hemolysis such as autoimmune hemolytic anemia also produces them. The DAT helps tell the two apart. Reference: Phillips & Henderson, Hemolytic Anemia: Evaluation and Differential Diagnosis, AFP 2018 (aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2018/0915/p354.html).

subject: HEMA
stem: Target cells (codocytes) are commonly seen in:
choices: Thalassemia, hemoglobin C and liver disease
explanation: Target cells appear in hemoglobin C disease or trait, thalassemias and liver disease (cholestasis). Reference: Peripheral Blood Film: A Review, Ann Ib Postgrad Med 2014 (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4415389).

subject: HEMA
stem: An increased RDW indicates:
explanation: The RDW is an index of variation in red cell size (anisocytosis). Reference: Anemia in Children, AFP 2001 (aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2001/1015/p1379.html).

subject: HEMA
stem: Schistocytes (fragmented red cells) are typical of:
explanation: Schistocytes come from red cells cut up within the vessels in microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (e.g. DIC, TTP, HUS). Reference: Phillips & Henderson, Hemolytic Anemia: Evaluation and Differential Diagnosis, AFP 2018 (aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2018/0915/p354.html).

subject: HEMA
stem: Heinz bodies are composed of:
explanation: Heinz bodies are denatured hemoglobin, seen in oxidant injury such as G6PD deficiency. DNA = Howell-Jolly bodies; iron = Pappenheimer bodies; RNA = basophilic stippling. Reference: Peripheral Blood Film: A Review, Ann Ib Postgrad Med 2014 (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4415389).

subject: HEMA
stem: Pappenheimer bodies are composed of:
explanation: Pappenheimer bodies are siderotic (iron) granules: purple on Romanowsky stain and blue on Perls (Prussian blue) stain. Reference: Peripheral Blood Film: A Review, Ann Ib Postgrad Med 2014 (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4415389).

subject: HEMA
stem: Coarse basophilic stippling is classically associated with:
explanation: Basophilic stippling represents aggregated ribosomes and is seen in lead poisoning, thalassemia and iron deficiency. Reference: Anemia in Children, AFP 2001 (aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2001/1015/p1379.html).

subject: HEMA
stem: Rouleaux formation on a blood smear is associated with:
explanation: Rouleaux (red cells stacked like coins) suggest a paraproteinemia or plasma cell dyscrasia such as multiple myeloma. Reference: Peripheral Blood Film: A Review, Ann Ib Postgrad Med 2014 (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4415389).

subject: HEMA
stem: Hereditary spherocytosis is characterized by spherocytes, a family history, and:
explanation: Hereditary spherocytosis has spherocytes, a family history and a negative DAT. Osmotic fragility (or EMA binding) testing confirms it. Reference: Phillips & Henderson, Hemolytic Anemia: Evaluation and Differential Diagnosis, AFP 2018 (aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2018/0915/p354.html).

subject: HEMA
stem: In hemoglobin S, which amino acid substitution occurs at position 6 of the beta chain?
explanation: In HbS, valine replaces glutamic acid at position 6 of beta-globin (Glu6Val). In HbC, lysine replaces glutamic acid at the same position. Reference: MedlinePlus Genetics, HBB gene (medlineplus.gov/genetics/gene/hbb).

subject: HEMA
stem: Microcytosis with HbA2 above about 3.5% suggests:
explanation: Beta-thalassemia trait causes microcytosis and mild anemia with elevated HbA2. Iron deficiency can lower HbA2 into the normal range. Reference: Muncie & Campbell, Alpha and Beta Thalassemia, AFP 2009 (aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2009/0815/p339.html).

subject: HEMA
stem: Hemoglobin Bart's (gamma-4) in large amounts at birth is associated with:
choices: Hydrops fetalis from deletion of all four alpha-globin genes
explanation: Deletion of all four alpha-globin genes produces large amounts of hemoglobin Bart's, causing nonimmune hydrops fetalis, usually fatal without treatment. Reference: Muncie & Campbell, Alpha and Beta Thalassemia, AFP 2009 (aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2009/0815/p339.html); Alpha- and Beta-thalassemia: Rapid Evidence Review, AFP 2022 (aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0300/p272.html).

subject: HEMA
stem: Bite cells and blister cells after an oxidant stress (for example, certain drugs) most suggest:
explanation: Bite and blister cells point to oxidative hemolysis, such as glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency. Reference: Phillips & Henderson, Hemolytic Anemia: Evaluation and Differential Diagnosis, AFP 2018 (aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2018/0915/p354.html).

subject: HEMA
stem: Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria is confirmed by flow cytometry showing loss of:
explanation: PNH cells lack GPI-anchored proteins, including the complement inhibitors CD55 and CD59, so complement lyses them. Flow cytometry is the diagnostic test. Reference: Update on the diagnosis and management of paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6142517).

subject: HEMA
stem: Pancytopenia with a hypocellular (fatty) bone marrow is characteristic of:
explanation: Aplastic anemia is pancytopenia with a hypocellular bone marrow that is not caused by infiltration or another disease. Reference: Approach to the diagnosis of aplastic anemia (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8270669).

subject: HEMA
stem: Anemia of chronic inflammation typically shows:
choices: Low iron, high TIBC, low ferritin
Low iron, low TIBC, normal or high ferritin
High iron, low TIBC, high ferritin
Normal iron, high TIBC, low ferritin
explanation: Anemia of chronic disease shows low serum iron with decreased TIBC, while ferritin is normal or high because it is an acute-phase reactant. Iron deficiency has low ferritin and high TIBC. Reference: Van Vranken, Evaluation of Microcytosis, AFP 2010 (aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2010/1101/p1117.html).

subject: HEMA
stem: The Philadelphia chromosome, t(9;22) with BCR-ABL1, is the hallmark of:
explanation: The Philadelphia chromosome, a reciprocal translocation of chromosomes 9 and 22 forming BCR-ABL1, is found in about 95% of patients with CML. Reference: Leukemia: What Primary Care Physicians Need to Know, AFP 2023 (aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2023/0400/leukemia.html); Leukemia: An Overview for Primary Care, AFP 2014 (aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2014/0501/p731.html).

subject: HEMA
stem: Acute promyelocytic leukemia with t(15;17) is especially dangerous because of its risk of:
explanation: APL with t(15;17) causes a severe coagulopathy with rapid consumption of clotting factors and platelets (DIC), so bleeding risk is immediate. Reference: Pathogenesis and Treatment of Thrombohemorrhagic Diathesis in Acute Promyelocytic Leukemia (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3248345).

subject: HEMA
stem: A leukemoid reaction is a very high white cell count (above about 50,000/uL) caused by:
choices: A reactive cause outside the bone marrow, such as severe infection
explanation: A leukemoid reaction is a WBC count above about 50,000 from a cause outside the marrow, not a leukemia. Reference: Abramson & Melton, Leukocytosis: Basics of Clinical Assessment, AFP 2000 (aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2000/1101/p2053.html).

subject: HEMA
stem: Many smudge (basket) cells on a smear of an older adult with lymphocytosis suggest:
explanation: Fragile CLL lymphocytes break when the smear is made; the degenerated nuclei are called smudge cells. Reference: Abramson & Melton, Leukocytosis: Basics of Clinical Assessment, AFP 2000 (aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2000/1101/p2053.html).

subject: HEMA
stem: Which flow cytometry marker is specific for hairy cell leukemia (and its variant) among B-cell neoplasms?
explanation: CD103 is specific for hairy cell leukemia and its variant; CD103 with bright CD123 points to classic HCL. Reference: Characteristic CD103 and CD123 Expression Pattern Defines Hairy Cell Leukemia (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7371092).

subject: HEMA
stem: A positive myeloperoxidase (MPO) stain on blasts helps distinguish:
explanation: MPO or Sudan black B positivity in 3% or more of blasts has been the cytochemical criterion for AML; lymphoblasts are usually negative. Reference: Sudan Black B Positive Acute Lymphocytic Leukemia (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4923274).

subject: HEMA
stem: Reed-Sternberg cells are the diagnostic cells of:
explanation: Hodgkin lymphoma is defined by characteristic multinucleated giant cells (Hodgkin and Reed-Sternberg cells) or their large mononuclear variants. Reference: NCI PDQ, Childhood Hodgkin Lymphoma Treatment, Health Professional Version (cancer.gov/types/lymphoma/hp/child-hodgkin-treatment-pdq).

subject: HEMA
stem: Pelger-Huet anomaly shows neutrophils with:
explanation: Pelger-Huet neutrophils have dumbbell-shaped bilobed ("pince-nez") nuclei with fewer segments, from LBR gene mutations; cell function is normal. Reference: Familial Pelger-Huet Anomaly (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4925487).

subject: HEMA
stem: Burkitt lymphoma is associated with:
explanation: t(8;14)(q24;q32), present in most cases, places the MYC gene next to the immunoglobulin heavy chain enhancers, driving very fast growth. Reference: An update on Burkitt lymphoma: a review of pathogenesis and multimodality imaging (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6529494).

subject: HEMA
stem: Which factor is measured by the PT but NOT by the aPTT?
explanation: The PT depends on fibrinogen and factors II, V, VII and X. The aPTT reflects the intrinsic and common pathways, so factor VII is the one tested only by the PT. Reference: Updates on Anticoagulation and Laboratory Tools for Therapy Monitoring of Heparin, VKAs and DOACs (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7998518).

subject: HEMA
stem: Unfractionated heparin therapy is commonly monitored with the:
explanation: The aPTT reflects the intrinsic and common pathways and is prolonged by heparin. Warfarin is monitored with the PT/INR. Reference: Updates on Anticoagulation and Laboratory Tools for Therapy Monitoring of Heparin, VKAs and DOACs (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7998518).

subject: HEMA
stem: The vitamin K-dependent coagulation factors are:
explanation: Warfarin antagonizes vitamin K, which is needed to make factors II, VII, IX and X (and proteins C and S). Reference: Horton & Bushwick, Warfarin Therapy: Evolving Strategies in Anticoagulation, AFP 1999 (aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/1999/0201/p635.html).

subject: HEMA
stem: Abnormal platelet aggregation ONLY with ristocetin points to:
choices: von Willebrand disease or Bernard-Soulier syndrome
explanation: Ristocetin-induced aggregation depends on vWF and GP Ib, so it detects both von Willebrand disease and Bernard-Soulier syndrome. Reference: Platelet function tests: a comparative review (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4340464).

subject: HEMA
stem: Glanzmann thrombasthenia is caused by a defect in:
explanation: Glanzmann thrombasthenia is a defect of GP IIb/IIIa (alphaIIb-beta3). Aggregation fails with all agonists, while ristocetin agglutination is usually preserved. Reference: Nurden, Glanzmann thrombasthenia, Orphanet J Rare Dis 2006 (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1475837).

subject: HEMA
stem: Factor XIII stabilizes a blood clot by:
explanation: Activated factor XIII is a transglutaminase that cross-links fibrin chains, making the clot stable. Thrombin converts fibrinogen to fibrin. Reference: Factor XIII Deficiency: A Review of Biology, Testing, and Treatment (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825037).

subject: HEMA
stem: D-dimer is a degradation product of:
explanation: D-dimer is produced when plasmin digests fibrin that was cross-linked by factor XIIIa. Reference: D-dimer Testing in Pulmonary Embolism with a Focus on Potential Pitfalls (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9689068).

subject: HEMA
stem: Which test detects factor XIII deficiency, which leaves the PT and aPTT normal?
explanation: FXIII deficiency gives a normal PT and aPTT. The 5 M urea clot solubility test is a classic screen, but it only detects severe deficiency, so quantitative FXIII activity is now the recommended first test. Reference: Factor XIII Deficiency: A Review of Biology, Testing, and Treatment (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12825037).

subject: HEMA
stem: The main reason for following the recommended order of draw is to:
explanation: Following the order of draw reduces carryover of additives from one tube to the next, which can cause wrong results. Reference: Standards and Practice Guidelines for Venous Blood Collection, Korean Society for Laboratory Medicine (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12187494).

subject: HEMA
stem: Reticulocytes are counted after staining with:
explanation: Supravital dyes such as new methylene blue or brilliant cresyl blue make the leftover RNA in reticulocytes visible. Reference: Reticulocyte count: a simple test but tricky interpretation! (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8490160).

subject: HEMA
stem: A sickle solubility test can be falsely NEGATIVE in:
choices: Young infants with high fetal hemoglobin
explanation: The test needs enough HbS; it can be falsely negative in infants with high HbF or when HbS is below about 10%. Reference: Sickle cell trait diagnosis: clinical and social implications (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4697437).

subject: HEMA
stem: The ICSH reference method for measuring hemoglobin is the:
explanation: The ICSH recommends the Drabkin method, which converts hemoglobin into cyanmethemoglobin and reads it photometrically. Reference: Breaking Free From MCHC Interferences? GFHC review (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12426809).

subject: HEMA
stem: Per CLSI order of draw, which of these tubes is drawn LAST?
explanation: Order: blood culture, light blue (citrate), red/gold (serum), green (heparin), lavender (EDTA), then gray (fluoride/oxalate). Reference: Standards and Practice Guidelines for Venous Blood Collection, Korean Society for Laboratory Medicine (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12187494).

subject: HEMA
stem: Which reagent, a bacterial toxin variant that binds GPI anchors, is used in flow cytometry for PNH?
explanation: FLAER is a fluorescently labeled inactive proaerolysin that binds GPI anchors. PNH cells lack GPI anchors, so they do not bind it. Reference: Update on the diagnosis and management of paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6142517).

subject: HEMA
stem: A positive sickle solubility (dithionite) test appears as:
choices: A clear solution with visible lines
A red precipitate at the bottom
explanation: With a reducing agent such as sodium dithionite, HbS becomes insoluble and the solution turns turbid. The test cannot tell sickle cell trait from disease. Reference: Sickle cell trait diagnosis: clinical and social implications (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4697437).

subject: HEMA
stem: An underfilled EDTA tube (excess EDTA) can cause a falsely HIGH:
explanation: Excess EDTA shrinks red cells, which results in an increased MCHC. Reference: Breaking Free From MCHC Interferences? GFHC review (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12426809).
